books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series (Economic Report of the President, Table B-22)

stimulus.text:
| Year | Unemployment rate |
| 1929 | 3.2% |
| 1930 | 8.7% |
| 1931 | 15.9% |
| 1932 | 23.6% |
| 1933 | 24.9% |

Unemployment as a share of the civilian labor force, 1929–1933.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series, as published in the Economic Report of the President, Table B-22.

source: original; stimulus table built from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series

options.misconception: The table shows the rate rising every year, from 3.2 percent to 24.9 percent. It did not fall.
The rate rose from 3.2 percent to 24.9 percent. It did not stay the same.
The rate passed 10 percent in 1931 and kept rising, reaching 24.9 percent in 1933.

options.text: rose to about one in four

rationales.A: The table shows 3.2 percent in 1929 and 24.9 percent in 1933, a rise, not a fall.
rationales.B: The table shows the rate climbing every year from 1929 to 1933.
rationales.C: The table shows 15.9 percent in 1931, already past 10 percent, and 24.9 percent by 1933.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the rate reached 24.9 percent in 1933, about one worker in four, the highest in American history.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first row: 3.2 percent in 1929.
2. Read the last row: 24.9 percent in 1933, the worst year of the Depression.
3. Ask what 24.9 percent means: about one worker in four.
4. The rate rose to about one in four.
Remember: a percent is a share, so turn it into people before judging how bad it was.
